analysis.title: Global Macro Monthly: Who Wants Duration?
key_insights: Central banks are reducing their footprint in long-dated government debt and Japanese investors have stronger incentives to keep capital at home, leaving long bonds more dependent on price-sensitive buyers who require higher yields to absorb duration.
TS Lombard remains a reluctant buyer of duration: growth is still firm and term premia offer limited compensation for uncertainty. A decisive slowdown would improve the case for long bonds.

US September payrolls rose only 29,000, unemployment reached 4.2% and wage growth slowed to 0.1% MoM. TSL still sees the labour market as having turned the corner and expects quarterly Fed hikes into 2027.
An October Fed hike is unlikely after the 25bp September move. Terminal rate pricing is now much closer to TSL's own view.

AI capex is supporting US activity through data centres, computing equipment and infrastructure, and higher equity prices feed household wealth. The current phase is more supportive of demand than disinflationary, with pressure building in power and semiconductor supply chains.
TSL is cautious on adding duration while US capex stays firm and the labour market stabilises. A sharp reversal in AI spending would weaken demand and equity wealth but is not the central case.

China is moving to a more supportive policy phase. Infrastructure bond issuance rose 60% MoM in August with about 45% of the annual quota still available, so fiscal policy should shift from a drag to a positive contribution.

The PBoC cut the pledged supplementary lending rate and expanded its re-lending quota by RMB200 billion. US-China relations have found a firmer floor with tariff implementation delayed. TSL keeps its 2026 China growth forecast at 4.8%.
Stronger Chinese activity reduces the likelihood of the synchronised global slowdown needed to pull bond yields materially lower.
Euro Area growth should firm as German fiscal expansion reaches the economy, with spare capacity in manufacturing and construction allowing output gains before much domestic inflation.

The ECB deposit rate reached 2.5% in September, with December more likely than October for the next move. TSL's base case is a 3% terminal rate in 2027, reached by March if energy pressures persist, or by H2 2027 if energy prices normalise.

France is the main regional bond market risk. The 10-year OAT-Bund spread briefly reached about 159bp before retracing. Around 140-150bp the trade becomes less one-way, and 200bp is the next significant level if the political process breaks down.
Le Pen's proposed path to a 3.7% deficit next year would require about €86 billion of tightening relative to unchanged policy, and several proposed savings are hard to verify.

Japan's Bank of Japan has moved into a faster tightening phase, with TSL's base case at roughly one hike every three months and a terminal rate around 2%. Japanese investors have been net sellers of long-term foreign debt over the past twelve months.

The Government Pension Investment Fund's domestic bond allocation rose to 27% by end of March. French bonds are Japan's largest European sovereign holding and second largest foreign bond position after US Treasuries, and recent Japanese purchases have tilted toward Bunds over OATs, leaving France exposed to repatriation.

UK August inflation rose to 3.1% with core at 2.6% and services at 3.4%. Private-sector regular wage growth is about 2.9% and vacancies continue to fall. A one-off BoE credibility hike is possible but sustained tightening is a poor fit with the labour data.
The Bank of England stopped selling the longest-dated Gilts at its September Asset Purchase Facility decision, acknowledging that defined-benefit pension demand has faded.

Across markets: US Treasuries keep the deepest buyer base, Bunds retain safe haven demand, OATs must compensate for political uncertainty, the UK long end is more price sensitive, and Japan is rebuilding domestic demand at the expense of foreign bonds.
TSL growth forecasts: US 2.5% in 2026 and 2027, China 4.8% and 4.4%, Euro Area 1.0% and 1.4-1.5%.

In the US, a 5%+ 10-year yield combined with rising debt reliance would make the AI investment cycle more sensitive to tighter financing. The main threat is that the economy overheats and the Fed has to slow the build-out.

tension_points.bull_case: A decisive global slowdown would improve the case for long bonds, and term premia remain modest relative to risks.
tension_points.bear_case: Firm US growth, AI capex, Chinese fiscal support and German spending, plus fading central bank, pension and Japanese demand, mean the marginal buyer keeps asking for more compensation.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A decisive slowdown in growth would improve the case for long bonds.

tension_points.bull_case: AI capex supports activity and equity wealth effects offset tighter bond conditions.
tension_points.bear_case: A sharp reversal in AI spending would weaken demand and wealth, and a 5%+ 10-year yield would make the cycle sensitive to tighter financing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A 5%+ 10-year yield or a sharp reversal in AI spending.

tension_points.bull_case: Around 140-150bp the trade becomes less one-way as markets anticipate a policy response.
tension_points.bear_case: The fiscal problem is unresolved and weaker Japanese demand adds pressure, with further widening possible if negotiations deteriorate.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Breakdown of the political process would push the spread toward 200bp.

theme_stances.key_argument: The marginal buyer of long-dated government debt is increasingly price sensitive and will keep asking for more compensation until growth slows decisively.
theme_stances.evidence: Until then, the marginal buyer is likely to keep asking for more compensation.

theme_stances.key_argument: Fading Japanese demand leaves France unusually exposed as political uncertainty meets a less forgiving buyer base.
theme_stances.evidence: leaving France unusually exposed if repatriation accelerates

theme_stances.key_argument: Weak September payrolls remove an October hike, but labour demand is expected to improve and keep quarterly hikes in place into 2027.
theme_stances.evidence: keep policymakers on a quarterly tightening path
